opts: Harmful things added to air, water or land faster than nature can clear them
quiz.why: Pollution covers air, water and land, and it comes from many sources, not only factories. Picking 'only smoke from factories' misses vehicles, burning rubbish, cooking smoke and sewage.

quiz.p: Which of these puts the most soot into a city's air?
quiz.why: Diesel engines burn fuel and give off soot. Bicycles burn nothing. Electric trains make no smoke on the street, though the power station that makes their electricity may.

quiz.p: Arjun, a boy in Coimbatore, leaves a sticky card on his window sill for three days. Another card stays in a closed dabba. The dabba card stays white. What does that show?
opts: The specks on the sill card came from the air
The dabba made the card cleaner
The jelly turns grey by itself
quiz.why: Both cards had the same jelly. Only the sill card met the air, and only it got specks. So the air brought them.

quiz.p: Why do scientists count the specks in only one corner of the square?
opts: It is quicker, and they can multiply by 4 for the whole square
The other corners are always empty
The corner is the dirtiest part
quiz.why: When specks are spread fairly evenly, a quarter of the square holds about a quarter of them. Counting a part and multiplying saves time.

quiz.p: What catches dust inside your nose?
quiz.why: Hairs catch the bigger dust, and sticky mucus catches smaller dust. The mucus is then swept out.

quiz.p: Which particles in smoke are the most harmful to lungs?
opts: The finest ones, too small to see
The biggest ones, which you can see
quiz.why: The nose catches big dust. The finest particles slip past it and reach deep into the lungs. Picking 'the biggest' is a natural guess, because we can see those.

quiz.p: In the soil test, muddy salt water went through soil. What came out?
opts: Clearer water that still had the salt in it
quiz.why: Soil stops pieces like mud, but dissolved salt goes through. That is why dissolved chemicals on the ground can reach groundwater.

quiz.p: What is the biggest cause of dirty rivers in India?
quiz.why: Sewage pours into many rivers without being cleaned. Microbes feeding on it use up the oxygen that fish need.

quiz.p: Why is a coat of dust a problem for a plant?
opts: It blocks light the leaves need to make food
It makes the plant grow too fast
It makes the leaves fall in one day
quiz.why: Leaves make food from sunlight. Dust blocks some light and can clog the tiny holes in the leaf.

quiz.p: On a dusty balcony, which kind of leaf lets dust slide off most easily in the rain?
opts: A smooth, waxy leaf, like a money plant leaf
A hairy leaf, like a tulsi leaf
A leaf with no water on it
quiz.why: Water runs off a smooth, waxy leaf and carries dust with it. Hairs hold on to dust.

quiz.p: Which change makes less smoke, instead of moving it somewhere else?
opts: Cooking on gas instead of wood
quiz.why: Gas burns much more cleanly than wood. Burning round the back or through a taller chimney still makes the same smoke.

quiz.p: Clair Patterson found almost no lead in very old Greenland ice, and much more in recent ice. What did this prove wrong?
opts: That the lead in the air was natural and had always been there
quiz.why: If the lead were natural, old ice would hold as much as new ice. The rise came after leaded petrol, so people had put it there.

items.p: Meenakshi, a girl in Class 3 in Madurai, wipes her window grill with a damp white cloth. The cloth comes away grey. Where did the grey come from?
opts: Dust and soot that came out of the air
items.why: Nobody put dirt on the grill. Dust and soot came out of the air, a speck at a time, and stuck to it. A strong answer says the dirt came from the air, and names a source such as vehicles or a building site.

items.p: Harmful things added to air, water or land faster than nature can clear them away are called ____.
items.why: Pollution is the word for it. One harmful thing, such as smoke, is called a pollutant.

items.p: Sort each one: does it mostly pollute the air, the water or the land?
items: smoke from a diesel lorry
Air
sewage poured into a river
Water
a rubbish heap on an empty plot
Land
dust from a building site
Air
washing a scooter in a lake
Water
plastic bags buried in a field
Land
items.why: Smoke and dust float in the air. Sewage and scooter washing go into the water. Rubbish and plastic stay on and in the ground. A strong answer notices that some things pollute more than one, such as burning rubbish, which dirties the air and leaves ash on the land.

items.p: In the Sticky Card Test, one card was shut in a closed steel dabba. Why?
opts: To show what a card looks like when the air cannot reach it
To keep it safe for later
To catch dust from inside the dabba
items.why: The dabba card is the control. It had the same jelly and stayed clean, so we know the specks on the other cards came from the air, not from the jelly or the card.

items.p: Lakshmi says, 'If the air looks clear, it must be clean.' Is she right?
items.why: False. Fine particles are too small to see one by one, and some harmful gases have no colour. The sticky card caught specks from air that looked clear.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: used water from toilets and kitchens
the sticky layer inside your nose
a grey look in the air from many fine particles
items.why: These four words come up all through the unit. A strong answer could also give an example of each.

items.p: Divya blows her nose after a day on a busy road. The tissue is grey. Why?
opts: The sticky mucus in her nose caught dust from the air
items.why: Mucus is sticky, like the jelly on the card. Every breath passes over it, and dust sticks. Dirtier air leaves more dust.

items.p: Name two things in or near your home that put smoke or dust into the air. For each one, say one way to make less.
items.a: For example: frying in the kitchen, so switch on the exhaust fan. Vehicles on the road, so switch the engine off at a signal.
items.why: A strong answer names real sources the child has seen, and a change that really reduces them, not just 'be careful'.

items.p: Which of these makes no smoke at all?
opts: Putting dry leaves in a compost pit
Burning dry leaves in a small pile
items.why: Any burning makes smoke, whatever the size of the pile or the time. Leaves in a compost pit rot into soil.

items.p: Draw your three sticky cards after three days: the flat one on the sill, the upright one on the grill, and the one from the dabba. Shade each square as grey as it was.
items.a: The flat card darkest, the upright card lighter, the dabba card white.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the difference clearly and labels each card with where it was.
items.art: Three blank card outlines with empty squares, labelled A, B and C.

items.p: Smoke from a mosquito coil in a closed bedroom is a kind of air pollution.
items.why: True. A burning coil gives off fine smoke for hours. In a closed room, that smoke stays in the air you breathe all night. A mosquito net keeps mosquitoes off without any smoke.

items.p: The water stored under the ground, which borewells pump up, is called ____.
items.why: Groundwater is water that soaked down through soil and rock. Pollution on the ground can reach it.

items.p: Anjali's tulsi plant is on a covered balcony beside a busy road. Their leaves look grey. Why is the dust a problem for the plant?
opts: It blocks some of the sunlight the leaves use to make food
It makes the leaves taste bitter
items.why: A leaf makes food from sunlight, air and water. Dust blocks some of the light, so the plant makes less food. On a covered balcony, no rain washes it off.

items.p: Your upright card on the grill caught some specks, though nothing could fall onto it. Explain how they got there.
items.a: Some specks are so tiny that they hardly fall. They float in the air, and the wind blows them against the card, where they stick.
items.why: A strong answer says the specks were floating and carried sideways by the air, not falling.

items.p: Two sisters in Kochi talk about their neighbour, who burns the dry leaves from his garden every week.

views.says: Leaves are natural, so burning them is fine. It's not like burning plastic.
The smoke still goes into our window and our noses. It doesn't matter that the leaves are natural.

items.ask: Which sister do you agree with? Use what you found with the sticky cards. Then say one thing the other sister has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses evidence: smoke from any burning carries soot and fine particles, and the sticky card shows that what is in the air lands near and inside us. It also gives the other side its due: burning plastic is worse, because its smoke has poisons in it as well.
items.why: Both sisters have a point. Plastic smoke is more poisonous, but smoke from leaves is still full of fine particles that harm lungs. Composting leaves avoids the smoke altogether.

items.p: Kavya counts 40 specks in one corner of her sticky card's square. The square has four equal corners, and the specks are spread evenly. About how many specks are in the whole square?
items.why: One corner is a quarter of the square. If one quarter holds 40, the whole holds about 4 times 40, which is 160. Scientists count part of a sample and multiply in the same way.

items.p: Put the steps of the Sticky Card Test in order.
items: Count the specks in one corner of each square
Spread a thin layer of jelly in each square
Draw a square on each card
Put the cards in their places for three days
a: Draw a square on each card
Spread a thin layer of jelly in each square
Put the cards in their places for three days
Count the specks in one corner of each square
items.why: First mark where to look, then make it sticky, then let the air reach it, then count.

items.p: Your nose and your sticky card both catch dust. Write two ways they are alike, and one way they are different.
items.a: Alike: both are sticky, and both catch dust from the air passing over them. Different: the card keeps the dust, but the nose sweeps the dirty mucus out and makes fresh mucus.
items.why: A strong answer compares how they catch dust and what happens to the dust afterwards.

items.p: Three of these put fine particles into the air in a home. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: The incense stick, the coil and the frying all give off smoke. A fan only moves the air that is already there.

items.p: The smallest particles in smoke are the most harmful to our lungs.
items.why: True. The nose catches bigger dust. The finest particles, about 30 times thinner than a hair, can slip past and reach the deepest parts of the lungs.

items.p: Label the picture of the soil filter: soil, cotton plug, muddy salt water going in, water coming out.
items.a: Muddy salt water poured in at the top, soil in the upper half, cotton plug in the bottle neck, water dripping into the lower half.
items.why: A strong answer shows the water going down through the soil, and labels what the soil stops (mud) and what it lets through (dissolved salt).
items.art: An unlabelled drawing of a cut plastic bottle with the top half upside down in the bottom half, filled with soil, with four blank label lines.

items.p: In the soil test, the water came out clearer, but it left a white crust when it dried. What did the soil stop?
opts: The mud, but not the dissolved salt
The salt, but not the mud
items.why: Soil catches pieces like mud in the gaps between its grains. Salt was dissolved, in pieces far too small to catch, so it went through with the water.

items.p: A factory spills a chemical that dissolves in water onto the ground. A family nearby drinks water from a borewell. Use the soil test to explain why they should worry.
items.a: In the soil test, dissolved salt went straight through the soil with the water. A dissolved chemical could do the same and reach the groundwater, which the borewell pumps up.
items.why: A strong answer connects the dissolved salt in the test to the dissolved chemical, and follows the water down to the borewell.

items.p: Sort each change: does it make less smoke, or does it only move the smoke somewhere else?
items: putting leaves in a compost pit
Makes less smoke
burning rubbish behind the building instead of in front
Only moves the smoke
switching off the engine at a signal
Makes less smoke
a taller factory chimney
Only moves the smoke
cooking on gas instead of wood
Makes less smoke
items.why: A taller chimney or a fire round the back still makes the same smoke, so somebody else breathes it. Composting, switching off and cleaner fuel make less smoke in the first place.

items.p: Sana in Pune notices that the far hill is blurry every winter morning, but clear after rain. Why is it clearer after rain?
opts: Rain washes particles out of the air
items.why: Raindrops catch dust and soot as they fall and bring them to the ground. That is one way nature cleans the air.

items.p: Opening the kitchen window or running the exhaust fan while frying helps the air in the kitchen.
items.why: True. The fan or the open window carries the smoke outside, so less stays in the kitchen for people to breathe.

items.p: A family in Hyderabad argues about the mosquito coil in the bedroom.

views.says: Mosquitoes carry dengue. The coil keeps them away, so it keeps us safe.
The coil fills our room with smoke all night. We breathe it for hours.
We used to sleep under a net. No mosquitoes and no smoke.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give a reason from this unit. Then say what the others have right.
items.a: A strong answer sees that both dangers are real: dengue is serious, and coil smoke is full of fine particles. It may choose the net because it solves both problems, and it gives each person credit for their point.
items.why: This is a real trade-off. The mother is right that mosquitoes are dangerous. Ishita is right about the smoke. Paati's net removes both problems, though a net must be tucked in well to work.

items.p: Many people think the air inside a home is always cleaner than outside. Describe a test that would find out whether that is true in your home.
items.a: Put one sticky card in the kitchen and one on the window sill for the same three days, with the same jelly and square. Count the specks in one corner of each and compare.
items.why: A strong answer keeps everything the same except the place, says how long, and says how to compare the results.

items.p: Black particles from burning diesel, wood or rubbish are called ____.
items.why: Soot is what the black specks on the sticky card mostly are. It forms when something burns without enough air.

items.p: On the cotton from Gurpreet's leaf wipe, the top of the leaf was grey and the underside was nearly white. What does this tell us about most of the dust?
opts: It falls down and settles on surfaces that face up
It is made by the leaf
It floats up from the ground
items.why: Most dust is heavy enough to settle slowly, so it lands on tops. Only the finest specks float about and stick underneath.

items.p: Your card on the window sill was dark grey after three days. A friend's card, on the 14th floor in a quiet lane, was light grey. Give two reasons the results could be different.
items.a: For example: her lane has fewer vehicles, so less soot. Road dust is kicked up near the ground, so less reaches the 14th floor. It may have rained on her side of the city.
items.why: A strong answer gives two different, testable reasons, not just 'her home is cleaner'.

items.p: A factory builds a taller chimney, and the air near the factory gets cleaner. What has happened to the smoke?
opts: The wind carries it further away, so other people breathe it
The tall chimney destroys the smoke
The smoke turns into clean air higher up
items.why: A taller chimney puts the smoke higher, where the wind spreads it over a wider area. The same amount of smoke is still made. It only lands somewhere else.

items.p: A building in Chennai is planning its Bhogi morning.

views.who: Lakshmi, who has lived there for 40 years
views.says: The bonfire is our tradition. My mother and grandmother lit it. Without the fire, it isn't Bhogi.
Last Bhogi my sticky card was the greyest it has ever been, and flights were stopped by the smoke.
Let's keep the fire small and burn only dry leaves and wood, never tyres or plastic.

items.ask: Whose plan would you choose? Use evidence from this unit. Then say what each of the other two has right.
items.a: A strong answer weighs the meaning of the tradition, the evidence from the sticky cards, and the smaller harm of a small, clean fire. It might choose a smokeless Bhogi or Farhan's middle way, and it respects Lakshmi's feeling for the tradition.
items.why: This is a real disagreement. Traditions matter to people. Smoke harms people. A small fire with no tyres or plastic makes far less harm, and a fire-free Bhogi makes none.

items.p: Some people say, 'The air belongs to nobody, so nobody has to keep it clean.' Others say, 'The air belongs to everybody, so everybody has to keep it clean.' What do you think? Use your nose and the sticky card in your answer.
items.a: A strong answer might say the air passes through every breathing body, so smoke made by one person ends up in other people's noses and lungs, which is why everyone has a share in keeping it clean.
items.why: A strong answer takes a side, gives a reason from the unit, and fairly states the other view.

items.p: Clair Patterson measured lead in layers of old Greenland ice. Snow from long ago had almost no lead, but recent snow had far more. What did this show?
opts: The lead in the air came from people, not from nature
Lead has always been in the air in the same amount
items.why: If the lead were natural, old snow would hold as much as new snow. It did not. The lead rose after people began burning leaded petrol.

items.p: Draw the path of one speck of soot from a bus exhaust to the inside of a child's nose. Show at least three places it passes.
items.a: For example: out of the exhaust pipe, up into the air over the road, blown towards a building, in through an open window, into the nose with a breath, caught in the mucus.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the soot floating and carried by the air, and ends with it caught by the mucus.
items.art: A blank space with a small bus on the left and a child's face on the right.

items.p: If a city puts all its rubbish in one big dump far away, the pollution is solved.
items.why: False. The rubbish is still there. Rain soaks through it into the groundwater, fires in the dump fill the air with smoke, and the people who live near the dump breathe it. Moving waste is not the same as making less of it.

items.p: Dust on a tree's leaves is hard for the tree. It also means less dust reaches people walking below. Is that fair to the tree? Say what you think and why.
items.a: A strong answer starts with the tree's own problem: dust blocks the light the leaves need to make food. It might say the tree pays a cost for people, and suggest ways people can help, such as making less dust or watering roadside trees.
items.why: A strong answer puts the tree's life first, then thinks about what people owe in return.

items.p: Sewage from a town pours into a river. Put what happens next in order.
items: Fish in the river run short of oxygen
Sewage pours into the river
Microbes in the water feed on the waste
The microbes use up oxygen in the water
a: Microbes in the water feed on the waste
The microbes use up oxygen in the water
Fish in the river run short of oxygen
items.why: The waste is food for microbes. As the microbes multiply and feed, they use the oxygen dissolved in the water, and fish need that same oxygen.

items.p: A shop says, 'Put two money plants in your bedroom and the air will be clean.' What do most recent studies say?
opts: A room would need far more plants than anyone keeps, so fresh air does much more
Two plants clean a room completely
items.why: In small sealed boxes, plants did take some gases out of the air. In a real room, air flows in and out all the time, and a few plants make only a tiny difference. Plants are good to live with for other reasons.

items.p: Fine particles are about ____ times thinner than a hair.
items.why: A hair is about 70 micrometres thick. The largest fine particles, PM2.5, are 2.5 micrometres. 70 divided by 2.5 is 28, so about 30 times.

items.p: Match each source to the main pollutant it adds.
pairs: A town's toilets with no treatment plant
A rubbish dump in the rain
dirty water soaking into the ground
items.why: Each source adds something different. A strong answer could add a second pollutant for some of them, such as plastic from the dump.

items.p: Children breathe more air for their size than grown-ups. Explain why this means dirty air affects children more.
items.a: More air for their size means more dust and soot passes into a child's nose and lungs for the size of their body. So the same dirty air puts a bigger load on a child.
items.why: A strong answer links more air breathed to more particles taken in, compared with body size.

items.p: Three of these help clean the air by themselves, without people doing anything. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Rain washes particles down, wind spreads smoke out, and leaves catch dust. A taller chimney does not clean anything. It sends the same smoke further away.

items.p: Revathi puts a sticky card on top of her kitchen cupboard for two days. It catches oily, sticky specks. Where did they most likely come from?
opts: Frying and tadka on the stove
items.why: Hot oil gives off tiny droplets of oil and smoke. They float in the kitchen air and stick to high surfaces. That is why kitchen tops get sticky.

applications: Air quality monitors on city streets, which measure fine particles every hour and give the AQI.
Masks for people who work on building sites, in traffic or in dusty factories.
Sewage treatment plants, which clean used water before it goes into a river or the sea.
Filters in air purifiers and in the air intake of buses and cars.
Rules that stopped leaded petrol, and rules for cleaner diesel and fuel.
Trees planted along busy roads to catch dust.

open_questions.q: Exactly how do fine particles harm the brain and heart?
open_questions.why_open: Studies show more illness where there are more fine particles, and particles have been found in blood. How they cause the harm inside the body is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: How much of a city's air pollution comes from each source?
open_questions.why_open: Different studies of the same city give different answers, because sources change with the season, the weather and the year.

open_questions.q: How do plants that live by busy roads cope with dust year after year?
open_questions.why_open: Some roadside plants do well and others struggle. Scientists are still finding out which leaf features and other ways of living help them most.

open_questions.q: Is there any amount of fine particles in the air that is completely safe?
open_questions.why_open: Health studies have found harm even at low amounts. Scientists have not found a level below which there is no harm at all.

What did the sticky card say to the soot?
Why was the window sill so tired?
What did one nose hair say to the other?
jokes.a: We'd better stick together, there's dust coming.

jokes.a: It had no sense of direction, it went wherever the wind blew.

jokes.j: What is a tissue's least favourite day?

jokes.j: What did the river say to the plastic bag?
jokes.a: Please don't drift into my life.

jokes.j: Why did the bus feel embarrassed at the signal?
jokes.a: It let out a big black puff in front of everyone.

jokes.j: What does a magnifying glass say to a speck of soot?
jokes.a: I see you, even if nobody else does.

jokes.j: Why did the compost pit win the Bhogi prize?
jokes.a: It took all the old things and made no smoke.

jokes.j: Why did the borewell refuse the salty water?
jokes.a: It had already had its fill.

maths.problem: Kavya counts 35 specks in the top left corner of her window card's square. The square has 4 equal corners, and the specks look evenly spread. About how many specks are in the whole square?
maths.explain: One corner is a quarter of the square. If one quarter holds 35, four quarters hold 4 times 35. 4 times 35 is 140. Check: 35 + 35 + 35 + 35 = 140.
maths.context: This is about the Sticky Card Test, where you count specks in one corner of a square of jelly instead of the whole square.
maths.why_maths: Counting every speck would take too long. Counting a part and multiplying gives a good estimate quickly.

maths.problem: In one corner of each square, Meenakshi counted: card A on the sill, 35 specks. Card B upright on the grill, 12 specks. Card C in the dabba, 1 speck. How many more specks did card A catch than card B? Why might card C have 1 speck, not 0?
maths.answer: 23 more specks. Card C may have caught a speck while the card was being made, before it went in the dabba.
maths.explain: 35 minus 12 is 23. Card C shows what gets on a card without the outside air, such as a speck from the room while the jelly was spread. That is why a control is useful: it tells us how much to ignore.

maths.problem: Sana checked her city's AQI each morning. Monday 85, Tuesday 92, Wednesday 160, Thursday 110, Friday 70. It rained on Thursday night. Which morning had the dirtiest air? How much lower was Friday than Wednesday? What might explain Friday?
maths.answer: Wednesday had the dirtiest air. Friday was 90 lower. The rain on Thursday night probably washed particles out of the air.
maths.explain: The highest number, 160, is the dirtiest. 160 minus 70 is 90. Rain catches particles as it falls, so the morning after rain is often clearer.
maths.context: This is about Haze Watch, where you check how clear the air is each morning and write the AQI number if you can find it.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the numbers day by day shows a pattern, and a pattern points to a cause, such as the rain.

maths.problem: Resting quietly, a child of 8 breathes about 20 times a minute. How many breaths is that in 10 minutes? If every breath passes over the sticky mucus in the nose, which would catch more dust in 10 minutes: a child sitting still or a child running?
maths.answer: About 200 breaths in 10 minutes. The running child, because they breathe faster and deeper, so more air and more dust pass through their nose and lungs.
maths.explain: 20 breaths a minute for 10 minutes is 20 times 10, which is 200. Running makes you breathe faster and take in more air with each breath, so more dust comes in.
maths.context: This is about your nose, which catches dust from every breath, like the sticky card.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying shows how quickly small amounts add up: a little dust in each breath becomes a lot over many breaths.

roots.context: We have caught the air's dust on sticky cards, on leaves and in our own noses. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: After one day, your window card still looked white. After three days, its square was grey with specks. No single speck was big enough to notice, but together they covered the card. Pollution grows the same way, from small amounts added every day, until rain and wind cannot clear them.
deep_truth.habit: We look for pollution in big, dramatic things, like a black cloud from a chimney. But most of it builds up from tiny amounts, from every vehicle, stove and fire, each too small to notice on its own.
deep_truth.evidence: On day 2 the cards still looked almost white. By day 3 the window card was grey, while the card in the closed dabba stayed white, so the specks came from the air and had piled up over the days. Clair Patterson's Greenland ice showed the same thing over many years: lead from petrol, too little to see in one year's snow, building up layer after layer.

three.who_am_i: You are a body that air flows through all day. Some of what the air carries stays in you.
three.what_is_life: Every living thing that meets the air, from a crow to a tulsi plant, meets the same dust.
three.what_is_this_world: The air over a city is shared. Smoke made in one lane ends up in the breath of people far away.

roots.thread: There is one air over a city, the same air for every creature in it. Every breath is drawn from it: yours, the crow's on the window sill, and the air taken in by the neem tree's leaves. When one person burns a tyre, the smoke does not stay theirs. It spreads into that one air and comes back as many breaths, in many noses and on many leaves. One air, shared by countless lives, is a plain, everyday picture of the One becoming the many.

teachings.link: Jain teachers saw the air itself as full of life to be cared for. Smoke harms the beings who live by breathing, from the smallest insect to us.
The smoke from one fire never stays alone. It lands on window sills, on leaves, and on the inside of every nose nearby, as your sticky cards showed.

science.text: The nose, the airways and their mucus remove most of the bigger particles from the air we breathe. The finest particles reach the deepest air sacs of the lungs.
Some of the finest particles pass from the lungs into the blood. How much harm they do to the heart and brain over a lifetime is still being studied.

other_view.view: Air is a mixture of gases and particles. Sharing it does not make us one, any more than sharing a road does. Pollution is a problem of chemistry and health, to be solved with cleaner fuels, filters and fair laws, with no need for ideas about oneness.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if in a city flat today, with the materials listed. The Sticky Card Test uses card from an empty biscuit or medicine box, petroleum jelly or coconut oil, and a steel dabba as the control. A window sill on the road side of a city flat reliably catches visible specks within three days. On a high floor or a quiet lane there are fewer, so the step says to leave the cards two more days, or to rate the colour if counting is hard. A grown-up does the taping, because children must not lean out of windows, and the card goes under the sunshade if rain is likely, because rain washes dust off. Counting one corner of the square keeps counting to a few minutes. The Leaf Wipe needs one potted plant that has stood near a window for a week, which most flats have. The soil filter needs a cut bottle, done by a grown-up, and two cups of soil from a pot. Two teaspoons of salt in a glass leave a thick white crust when a spoonful dries in the sun in a few hours, and the step gives a faster tawa method for a cloudy day. Nobody tastes any water. Your Nose, the Dust Catcher depends on the day: a tissue may stay white after a trip in clean air, and the step says that is good news. Source Snap works for one child alone. The spine (intro, the White Cloth Wipe, the Sticky Card Test, the explanation cards, Roots and the quiz) fits about 85 minutes over two sessions, with the cards left out for three days in between.

how_we_found_out.story: In the 1950s, Clair Patterson, an American scientist, set out to measure the age of the Earth from tiny amounts of lead in rocks. He kept getting wrong results, because lead from the air was getting into his samples. It was on the dust, his tools, even his hands. So he built one of the world's first very clean labs, with filtered air and scrubbed surfaces, and found the Earth's age: about 4.55 billion years. But a question stayed with him. Where was all that lead in the air coming from? Most experts, such as Robert Kehoe, who worked with the makers of leaded petrol, said the lead in air and in people's bodies was natural and had always been there. Patterson tested this. With his co-workers Masayo Murozumi and Tsaihwa Chow, he measured lead in ice from deep in the Greenland ice sheet. Each year's snow is a layer, so old layers hold old air. Snow from long ago had almost no lead. Recent layers had far more, and the rise was steepest after leaded petrol came into use. The lead was not natural. Countries slowly stopped selling leaded petrol. India stopped in 2000, and the whole world had stopped by 2021.
how_we_found_out.who: Clair Patterson, an American scientist, with his co-workers Masayo Murozumi and Tsaihwa Chow; Robert Kehoe, who held the opposite view
how_we_found_out.when: 1950s (the clean lab and the Earth's age), 1965 (Patterson's warning about lead), 1969 (the Greenland ice results)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Most experts said the lead in the air and in people's bodies was natural and had always been there. Layers of old Greenland ice showed that there had been almost no lead in the air before people began burning leaded petrol.
how_we_found_out.art: A scientist in a white coat in a clean lab holding up a long cylinder of ice with layers in it, and a small picture of an old car's exhaust beside it.
